newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW-L.Ashley forced to mark down stock.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-L.Ashley forced to mark down stock.

text.p: British retailer Laura Ashley Holdings Plc on Thursday blamed over-ambitious sales plans for forcing stock mark-downs, bringing lower than expected earnings for the current year.
Chief executive Ann Iverson said a smaller number of new store openings in North America, plus aggressive sales plans, had left the group overstocked with garments.

"We will open less stores in the first half in North America than we had bought to," she said in a telephone interview. "Also we had a very aggressive sales plan in merchandising in the first half and it was too aggressive frankly and the business wasn't ready for it."

The firm earlier warned that profits in the current year, while ahead of last year, would be below current market expectations. Analysts were forecasting pre-tax profits in 1997/98 of between 22 million and 23 million stg. Last year Laura Ashley raised profits by 57 percent to 16.2 million stg.

Iverson said the group would mark down stock to ensure it was cleared by the end of the season. But she said the stock problem was due to overbuying and not "a concern on the design direction in any way that we are taking."

Iverson said she was confident that the design strategy of the group was not the problem. Last year the firm moved to update its trademark floral print look, following the appointment of Basha Cohen as the new director of design and buying.
"I support very much what is being done and I believe my strategy is correct," Iverson said.
Iverson, who made her name in Britain by turning around Storehouse's Mothercare chain, said her recovery programme for Laura Ashley was intact.
"I think the UK trading has continued to be strong while we have gone through significant, massive change in this organisation last year."
She said it would be a three to four year process to reposition the company and to see it begin earning double digit margins.
"I'll be here two years this summer - I'm really pleased with the progress we've made."
She said the aim was to keep tight control of costs, but exchange rate pressures meant people were "running hard to stand still."

The group said manufacturing had become more competitive during the past year. "We have always said that it is imperative they be competitive. If they weren't, we wouldn't buy from them," Iverson said.
She said the group would continue to look at ways to reduce costs in manufacturing and monitor it very closely.
The shares fell steeply after the profit-warning and stood 30 pence lower at 115 pence by 0832 GMT.
